assessment.nobel_worthiness: A clean, general mechanism: spin-orbit coupling plus time-reversal symmetry gives a Z2 topological classification and protected edge or surface states. Kane and Mele turned a messy band-structure problem into a simple, rigorous theory, and it opened a whole field of topological matter that reaches into photonics and cold atoms.
assessment.attribution: Kane and Mele made the decisive theoretical step (graphene quantum spin Hall, Z2 invariant). Molenkamp's group gave the first experimental quantum spin Hall realization in HgTe/CdTe, following the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang proposal. Hasan's 3D topological insulator work is also decisive, but three seats cannot hold everyone, so I propose two theorists and the first experimentalist. The BHZ proposal sits outside the credited names, which makes the theory-experiment link awkward.
assessment.maturity: Independently confirmed by transport and ARPES in many materials over about 18 years. The interpretation is stable and the recognition is timely, even a little overdue.
uncertainties: Credit is contested between the 2D and 3D branches, and between Kane-Mele and BHZ.
The prize can only cover three of the four credited names.
Overlap with the topological work already recognized in 2016 needs to be considered.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Fractional statistics in two dimensions is a profound conceptual advance: exchange statistics beyond bosons and fermions follows from the topology of configuration space. It is a clear universal mechanism and links to topological quantum computing. Experimental confirmation of fractional charge and of anyonic braiding is now in hand.
assessment.attribution: Leinaas and Myrheim (1977) first identified the possibility of intermediate statistics in low dimensions. Heiblum's group measured fractional charge by shot noise and drove the interferometric experiments. Fève and Manfra contributed to the later anyon collision and braiding experiments. Wilczek (who named anyons) and the Laughlin-type theory are outside the supplied credit, so the allocation is incomplete.
assessment.maturity: Fractional charge was confirmed repeatedly in the 1990s. Anyonic exchange statistics were seen in collision and Fabry-Perot interferometer experiments around 2020. Further confirmation is still maturing but it is already strong.
uncertainties: Wilczek and others are missing from the supplied credit.
Interferometer results have had Coulomb-blockade confounds, and some later work was disputed.
It is unclear whether recognition is better after more non-Abelian evidence.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: A simple continuum model predicts a magic angle with flat bands, and experiments then found correlated insulators and superconductivity in the same system. The fit between a minimal theory and a surprising result is rare. It founded a large moire-materials field.
assessment.attribution: Bistritzer and MacDonald (2011) gave the flat-band prediction. Jarillo-Herrero's 2018 experiments established correlated insulators and superconductivity. Andrei independently saw related flat-band signatures but the three-person limit favours the theory pair plus the main experimentalist.
assessment.maturity: Reproduced by many groups. The origin of the superconductivity is still debated, so the mechanism is not understood. The discovery of the phenomenon is mature but the physics is still being explained.
uncertainties: Pairing mechanism unresolved.
Allocation among Andrei, Jarillo-Herrero and earlier theory (not credited here) is not clean.
Possibly a few years early for the full story.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Exact relations for work and entropy production far from equilibrium are the closest thing to universal laws in nonequilibrium statistical physics. They are simple, rigorous and general. They are also used experimentally to extract free energies from single-molecule pulling and in stochastic thermodynamics. This is directly in my own area.
assessment.attribution: Evans, Cohen and Morriss (fluctuation theorem), Jarzynski (1997 equality) and Crooks (1999 relation) are the core. Gallavotti-Cohen, Bochkov-Kuzovlev and Kurchan, Lebowitz-Spohn also have strong claims, and none of them are in the supplied credit, so the attribution is fragile.
assessment.maturity: Experimentally verified in optical tweezers, RNA unfolding and colloidal systems. The theory is mature. Impact is widespread in stochastic thermodynamics, though the experimental test cases are mostly in biophysics and chemistry.
uncertainties: Priority disputes, including omitted names, make a fair three-person split difficult.
Whether the committee sees this as physics with broad enough consequences.
Experimental tests are mostly near equilibrium or in small systems.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The funnel energy landscape explains how a protein with astronomically many conformations folds quickly. This uses spin-glass ideas (the random energy model, minimal frustration) in biology, and connects to the same statistical-mechanics view of learning recognized in 2024. It is an elegant physical answer to Levinthal's paradox.
assessment.attribution: Wolynes and Bryngelson laid down the funnel and spin-glass picture, with Onuchic as a close collaborator who developed it into predictive models. Dill's contributions (hydrophobic collapse, lattice models) are significant but differ in emphasis. Bryngelson is not credited, and that is an attribution gap.
assessment.maturity: The concept is accepted and underlies structure-prediction methods. It is validated by folding kinetics and simulations. However, it may be seen as adjacent to the 2024 Chemistry prize, which concerned structure prediction, and it fits the physics prize only partly.
uncertainties: Is it physics or chemistry or biology?
Bryngelson is missing from the credit.
Overlap with the 2024 prizes may reduce the priority.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: A beautiful extension of Kosterlitz-Thouless: two-step melting through dislocation unbinding and a hexatic phase, with predicted critical exponents. It is a textbook example of universality, and supported by experiments on colloids, films and many 2D systems.
assessment.attribution: Halperin and Nelson (1978) and Young (1979) are the theoretical architects. The credit is clean and compact. Kosterlitz and Thouless have already been recognized in 2016, so the lineage is well understood.
assessment.maturity: Verified in colloidal crystals, liquid crystals and simulations, though some cases show first-order melting. The theory is stable and has been mature for decades. Recognition is very late, which may reduce urgency.
uncertainties: Simulation and experiment sometimes show first-order melting.
The committee may consider it a continuation of the 2016 prize.
The relative contribution of Young is smaller.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: DMFT is the best controlled non-perturbative method for strongly correlated electrons. It resolves the Mott transition in infinite dimensions, and combined with DFT it is used for realistic materials. A mean-field theory that is exact in a limit is the kind of clean idea I find convincing.
assessment.attribution: Metzner and Vollhardt (1989) introduced the infinite-dimension limit, and Georges and Kotliar (1992) mapped it to an impurity problem. Müller-Hartmann and Metzner are not in the credit. Rozenberg and Jarrell had important parallel contributions.
assessment.maturity: Widely used, and verified through comparison with experiment on the Mott transition and with numerical methods. The method's limits (neglect of nonlocal correlations) are known. Mature, though a computational-method prize is unusual.
uncertainties: Method versus discovery, which the statutes may weigh differently.
Credit is spread among others, such as Metzner and Müller-Hartmann.
Limited agreement with experiment in low-dimension systems.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Ultracold atoms in optical lattices realize Hubbard models with tunable parameters, and the superfluid to Mott insulator transition and quantum gas microscopy give direct access to many-body physics. This links condensed matter theory to controllable experiments, and I value that.
assessment.attribution: Jaksch, Zoller and collaborators gave the Bose-Hubbard proposal, and Greiner, Bloch and Hänsch observed the transition in 2002. Esslinger did the Fermi-Hubbard work and Cirac has strong theoretical claims. Allocation across five names is difficult, and Zoller also appears in two other entries.
assessment.maturity: Very mature and widely reproduced. Recognition partly overlaps the 2001 BEC prize and the 2012 prize for quantum control of single systems, and the field is still moving toward quantum advantage claims.
uncertainties: Five credited names do not fit within three seats.
Jaksch is not in the credited list.
Overlap with earlier cold-atom prizes.
